text: We are flexible about the language we use.
But you should be able to write standard programs and implement some of the basic algorithms
that we are using in our course.
In order to do this, we will of course cover some new data structures in this course.
But we do expect that in the language that you use, you are familiar with basic
concepts like arrays and lists and also things like stacks and queues which build up on
these.
Of course, when we come to stacks and queues, we will try to give some detail about how
they are used.
But we do expect that you have seen them before.
So this is not the first time you are seeing these concepts.
Here is a kind of approximate list of the topics we expect to cover in the course.
So after looking at a few examples, we will start with asymptotic complexity, which is
the way of measuring the efficiency of an algorithm and writing down this measure in a
way that we can compare easily across algorithms.
We will then move to the most basic problem that we have for arrays, which is to search
and array for an element.
And in the process, we will realize that it's important to be able to sort the array
efficiently in order to arrange the elements in a way where we can search in an effective
manner.
So we will look at searching and sorting.
So we will look at binary search and we will look at different notions of sorting, some
of which are more elementary and intuitive like insertion, sort and selection, sort, but
are not the best in terms of efficiency.
And then we will look at more efficient algorithms like merge, sort and quick, sort, which are
not obvious to begin with.
Moving on from searching and sorting, we come to graphs and graph algorithms.
So we will introduce graphs.
We will see how we can use them to model certain types of problems.
We need to know how to represent a graph.
How do you, a graph is essentially a picture.
So how do you translate this picture into something that an algorithm can manipulate?
So that's representation.
We will look at standard problems and graphs, reachability and connectedness.
We will look at a special class of graphs called directed acyclic graphs, which are very
useful for modeling certain kinds of problems.
And then we will look at other canonical problems on graphs, including shortest paths
and spanning trees.
As we mentioned before, there are some basic algorithmic design techniques which apply across
a class of problems.
So we will look in particular at divide and conquer greedy algorithms and dynamic program.
Among the data structures that we will encounter in this course are priority cues, which are
often implemented through deeps.
You will look at binary search trees, which are efficient ways of maintaining information
and sorted order dynamically as information comes and goes.
And we will look at a very useful data structure to maintain a partition of a set into a disjoint
collection of subsets, the so-called union fine algorithm.
And finally, depending on how much time is left, we will look at the miscellaneous topics.
It is important to realize that not every algorithm admits an efficient solution.
So we will look at problems of interactability and some provably hard problems and some
other problems of which the status is unknown.
This is an eight week course.
The tentative schedule is as follows.
In the first week, we will do some motivating examples and we will look at some notations
and work out some problems involving asymptotic complexity.
In the second week, we will move on to searching and sorting.
In the third week, we will introduce graphs and look at basic graph algorithms.
We will continue with more graph algorithms and then in the process, introduce the disjoint
set data structure.
We will then formally look at divide and conquer, which we have already seen along the way,
but we will look at it again and then we will introduce heaps.
In the sixth week, we will do search trees and some examples of greedy algorithms and
their proofs.
The seventh week will be devoted to dynamic programming and in the last week, we will cover
miscellaneous topics.
Now you should remember that this is only an approximate schedule and there will be some
variations but roughly this is the sequence and the speed at which we plan to cover the
material in the course.
You can also see alongside the weeks, the calendar weeks that these correspond to.
So the first week of the course is the current week, which is January 5th to 9th and this
course will go on to the last week of February.
Now as part of the evaluation for the course, there will be continuous evaluation.
Every week, there will be quizzes.
There will also be programming assignments, roughly six programming assignments across
the eight weeks.
After the course ends, there will be a certification exam.
In order to get a certificate that you have successfully completed this course, you need
to score 60% in the quizzes and in the certification exam.
You need to submit at least five or six out of the six assignments and at least four of
them, you must do something non-trivial.
We will be following two main textbooks although I will not use the textbooks directly
in the course, but if you want to look up some material, you will find them in these
two books.
The first book is called Algorithm Design by John Kleinberg and A. Watt Ardosh.
And the second book is just called Algorithms by Svanjoy Daskuptha, Christos Papadimitro
and Humeishwai Srirani.
The book by Kleinberg and Tardosh is more detailed and it has a number of really nice examples
to illustrate many of the concepts and quite detailed proofs.
The book by Daskuptha, Papadimitro and Vasirani is a slimmer book.
It is more easy and accessible to read on your own, but on the other hand, it does leave
a lot of details as exercises.
So in order to really understand the material, you really need to spend more time working
out the exercises and not just go by the material that is presented in the chapters.
